deep_why: FG-Trac tracks individual data samples as they move through a machine learning pipeline by recording cryptographic checkpoints at each stage. The soundness comes from cryptography itself: if a record is attached to a tamper-evident commitment (a cryptographic hash tied to a specific time or checkpoint), then any alteration of the data breaks the hash, making tampering instantly detectable. This works because cryptographic commitments are one-way functions where two different inputs almost certainly produce different outputs. The framework can therefore reconstruct a complete, auditable history of which samples were used and when, letting practitioners verify that no data was silently dropped, duplicated, or modified between preprocessing and model training.

BARouter solves the problem of routing queries to different language models while staying within a total computational budget. The method works because it tracks the real-time cost spent so far and adjusts future decisions to consume the remaining budget wisely. Mathematically, this is sound because cost is additive: if you spend X now, you have Budget minus X left, and that remainder is certain. By always choosing routes that improve quality per unit cost spent (based on online feedback), the router guarantees it will not exceed the budget while steadily learning which routes give the best quality. Over time, the total regret—the gap between what it achieved and what the best fixed strategy would achieve—grows sublinearly, meaning the router catches up to optimal routing.

FakeAgent detects misinformation in micro-videos by analyzing both the video content itself and external evidence retrieved from the web, then reasoning across both together. The soundness lies in combining two independent signals: a video's visual and audio cues can be deceptive, but external sources (news archives, fact-checking sites) are harder to fake in coordination. When both the content analysis and the evidence analysis point to the same conclusion, that agreement acts as verification—a single deceptive source is unlikely to fool both an AI model seeing the video and independently retrieved evidence. This convergence of multiple reasoning paths from different information sources dramatically reduces the chance of false conclusions.

HyGRAG improves retrieval-augmented generation by building a hierarchical graph where related information is summarized at multiple levels of abstraction. The method works because summarization preserves the core meaning while compressing representation, so searching at higher abstraction levels is faster and captures relationships that chunk-level search alone would miss. When clusters of related content are summarized together, that summary fuses contextual and relational information in a single readable unit. During retrieval, searching across all abstraction levels means rare or deeply buried knowledge can still be found via its high-level category, not just shallow text similarity, and community membership allows expansion to logically linked content the similarity search never reached.

DIARY protects federated learning systems from two threats: model poisoning and gradient inversion attacks. It allocates a privacy budget adaptively across training and recovery phases, meaning it adds varying amounts of noise to gradients at strategic points to block attackers from reconstructing private data. This works because adding noise to gradients mathematically prevents exact reconstruction—the attacker sees only noisy signals, not the true values. By allocating the global privacy budget wisely (more noise where attacks are likely, less where utility matters most), the system stays within a formal privacy bound while recovering from poisoning. The FIND anomaly detection module identifies suspicious updates before they corrupt the model, so recovery is fast and the privacy budget is not wasted on unnecessary noise.

SORG generates pairs of opposing arguments (agree and disagree) about whether a news headline is clickbait, then trains a smaller model to use both perspectives as contrastive signals. The method works because a headline that is genuinely clickbait will have plausible-sounding both-sides arguments, but genuine arguments will pull in opposite directions on detection, creating a clear signal. When a model is trained on contrastive pairs—one labeled likely-clickbait, one likely-honest—it learns to separate the two classes not by memorizing keywords but by understanding why credible and deceptive headlines differ. This forces the model to discover the real patterns of deception rather than surface cues, making it more robust to new, unseen clickbait.

This study experimentally measures whether YouTube's feedback buttons actually reduce unwanted recommendations by having thousands of users trigger different feedback signals and observing what happens next. The soundness is statistical: with 567 million recommendations collected and a control group receiving no feedback, the researchers can measure the true causal effect of each button by comparing recommendation distributions before and after. Large-scale data is essential here because unwanted recommendations are rare, so without millions of samples, random variation would drown out the true effect. By comparing what actually appeared in recommendations (using a trained similarity model), the study reveals the ground truth: most feedback mechanisms fail because recommendations that are similar to disliked content still appear afterward.

The algorithm solves the problem of assigning users to options (arms) in a bandit setting while keeping each user anonymous—the central system learns which arm is best without learning who preferred it. The method works by using successive elimination: options that perform poorly are discarded, leaving only the best candidates. The greedy matching algorithm then assigns remaining users to remaining arms such that no user or option is revealed. Mathematically, successive elimination is sound because it samples options carefully to identify truly poor ones with high statistical confidence before ruling them out. By discarding only options that are demonstrably worse than others, the algorithm guarantees it explores enough to find near-optimal assignments without wasteful exploration, keeping regret sublinear.

HierCon detects audio deepfakes by modeling dependencies across layers of a pre-trained audio model—adjacent layers, frame sequences, and groups of related layers. The soundness comes from the observation that real speech has consistent artifact patterns across layers: a genuine human voice excites neural representations consistently from low to high levels. Synthetic speech generated by a text-to-speech system violates these patterns—layers conflict or show artificial uniformity. By learning how layers should relate in genuine speech (using contrastive learning to separate real from fake), the model captures these hierarchical dependencies as a fingerprint of authenticity. Domain-invariant embeddings further ensure this fingerprint generalizes to new deepfake generators, because the underlying inconsistency in synthetic speech remains regardless of the generator used.

This work designs websites where AI agents can be granted fine-grained access control, so they can perform delegated tasks on a user's behalf without being handed full account access. The soundness lies in separation of privilege: instead of giving an agent the user's password or full authorization, the website grants narrow permissions for specific actions (e.g., view billing, schedule appointment, but not change password). This is secure because the agent can only do what the permission allows, even if compromised or manipulated by an attacker. The authorization service tracks which agent received which permission for which task, making abuse traceable and revocable. Delegating critical tasks safely requires that each permission grant is tied to a specific task scope, so an agent cannot expand its authority beyond what the user explicitly approved.

This tutorial framework lays out foundations for a decentralized network of autonomous AI agents that can discover, negotiate, and coordinate with each other without a central authority. The reasoning is that the traditional web succeeded because DNS and HTTP established shared protocols for discovery and communication. Similarly, agent networks need registries (where agents advertise themselves), identity systems (so agents can prove who they are), and reputation mechanisms (so other agents know whom to trust). Without these, agents cannot find each other or verify each other's reliability. Markets and governance structures emerge naturally once the foundation is stable: agents trade services using reputation as currency, and populations self-coordinate through pricing signals. The architecture is sound because each layer (technical, economic, social) builds trustworthily on the layer below.

PADD detects jailbreak prompts by prepending a safety prefix to the input and comparing how the model's internal attention changes between the original and modified versions. The method works because a jailbreak is designed to manipulate the model into bypassing safety guardrails by shifting attention away from safety considerations. Adding a safety prefix re-weights the model's attention toward safety-relevant tokens. When you compare attention distributions (original vs. prefixed), a benign prompt shows stable attention patterns, while a jailbreak shows large divergence—the attacker's manipulation is undone by the safety prefix, exposing the adversarial structure. This divergence is detectable without external classifiers or retraining the model, making PADD fast and model-agnostic, because the attack leaves internal signatures of malice that surface when the safety prefix forces the model to reconsider.

The metacognitive framework monitors an ensemble of language models by computing a Metacognitive State Vector that tracks five psychological dimensions: emotional response, correctness, experience match, conflicting information, and problem importance. This works because uncertainty has multiple origins—some queries are genuinely hard (high problem importance), others reveal conflicting information across models, and some exceed all models' training data. By quantifying these dimensions explicitly, the system can route queries intelligently: simple, confident questions go to fast System 1 processing, while complex or conflicted questions escalate to deliberative System 2 reasoning with specialized roles. The soundness comes from cognitive psychology: humans use similar metacognitive monitoring to decide when to think slowly. Mirroring this in AI ensures the ensemble recognizes its own limits and escalates appropriately rather than confidently guessing.

All/any-k ANN search extends traditional nearest-neighbor search to multi-reference queries: find vectors similar to all references (intersection) or to any reference (union). The method works by defining distance metrics that score each candidate vector by how well it satisfies the all/any criterion, then using existing ANN graph indexes designed for single-reference search. Mathematically, the distance metrics preserve ordering: if vector A is more similar to all references than vector B, the metric assigns A a smaller distance. Because the underlying graph index (like HNSW) works by locally optimal distance comparisons regardless of the distance function used, the same graph structure that finds good neighbors for one reference can find good neighbors for multiple references. Two-stage search improves this by first filtering candidates coarsely, then refining with the full all/any metric, trading small accuracy loss for dramatic speedup.

PAMAS combats the information-drowning problem in multi-agent misinformation detection by organizing agents into three hierarchical roles and using perspective-aware aggregation. The soundness lies in specialization and filtering: instead of every agent seeing all information, Auditors each examine specific feature subsets (anomaly patterns, linguistic cues, network signals), so each agent finds what it is designed to detect without being overwhelmed. Coordinators then aggregate these specialized findings, weighting them to maintain diversity so weak deceptive cues are not lost in the flood of truthful content. The Decision-Maker combines all perspectives with evolving memory of patterns seen so far. This hierarchy works because a signal that is weak globally can be strong locally—an anomaly that appears rare overall might be systematic within a linguistic feature subset. By having agents specialize and coordinate hierarchically, the system recovers weak deceptive cues that flat, full-access architectures would drown out.
